issues.issue: The phrase "you, as successor-in-interest to DeNovo Music Group, Inc. and Steemer Corporation, respectively" uses "respectively" with a single addressee, so which entity's rights Malmsteen personally took, and in what capacity, is not stated. The Agreement it amends names DeNovo Productions as "Grantor," leaving unclear whether "you" in this letter is the Grantor bound by the operative paragraphs.

Only the first sentence of paragraph 1.02 was replaced, so the surviving option-exercise mechanics and the Minimum Recording Obligation schedule in paragraph 2.02 of the Agreement still contemplate three Option Periods only. Whether the fourth option carries the same exercise and Contract Period-end mechanics can only be answered by reading 1.02's unamended remainder with 2.02.

Paragraph 2.02's schedule of the Minimum Recording Obligation was never itself amended and lists no fourth Option Period, so this one-Album obligation exists only by the "notwithstanding" override. Whether the fourth Option Period's other incidents (Contract Period end under 1.01/1.02, delivery under 4.01) follow the two-Album pattern is left to be worked out against 2.02.

The requirement that the first Album of the first Option Period be "comprised entirely" of live Soviet-tour Master Recordings is followed by struck-through and hand-interlineated matter (apparently permitting additional non-live recordings), so the Album's permitted content cannot be read off the page. Whether "entirely" survives the alteration, and what the interlineation added, is precisely what a court would have to construe.

The label "Live Album" is fastened to the first Album of the first Option Period as described in the preceding, altered sentence of 3.06(b), so its content requirement is borrowed from a provision whose text is in doubt. Read with 4.01(a)(ii), which uses the same equation, the defined term may attach to an Album that is not in fact entirely live.

The single sentence gathers the Initial Period, the second and third Option Periods and the fourth Option Period and then fixes delivery at 120 days after "commencement of such Period," leaving the antecedent of "such Period" to be supplied for each listed Album. The Initial Period limb is also spent, since that Period ran from 1985 and this amendment is dated April 3, 1989.

The fixed May 29, 1989 date is stated without reference to when the first Option Period commences, yet under paragraph 1.02 of the Agreement PRI may exercise the option at any time before expiration of the current Period and under amended 6.01(b)(i) a quarter of the Advance falls due on commencement. The delivery date can therefore precede, or long follow, the events the payment and term provisions tie it to.

The limb governing the second Album of the Initial Period measures delivery from delivery of that Period's first Album, but the Initial Period began in 1985 and had run before this April 1989 amendment, so the window it creates is retrospective. Read with amended 4.01(a)(i), which likewise still fixes an Initial Period deadline, it is unclear whether these Initial Period limbs have any operation at all.

Disapplying the whole of paragraph 4.01(d) to the Live Album removes not only the sixty-day grace period in 4.01(d)(i) but also 4.01(d)(ii)'s suspension of the delivery date when the parties cannot agree on the co-producer under paragraph 3.02(i). Whether the parties meant to strip that co-producer protection as well is left open by the blanket cross-reference.

"The applicable amount set forth below" points to a table numbering Albums First through Ninth without tying any Album number to a Contract Period or to the Minimum Recording Obligation, so which figure is "applicable" to a given Album must be inferred. The problem is sharpened because this replacement table (nine Albums, differing amounts) supersedes the Agreement's eight-Album table.

The trigger "within sixty (60) days ... following the day of PRI's receipt of this agreement, fully executed by Grantor and Artist" was carried verbatim from the 1985 Agreement into this 1989 amendment, so "this agreement" may mean either instrument. On either reading the Initial Period trigger is already spent, leaving the timing of that quarter of the Advance uncertain.

Making Grantor responsible for "all Recording Costs or other costs in connection with making Master Recordings" sits awkwardly with amended 6.01(b)(i) and with paragraph 3.02 of the Agreement, which deems approved a budget equal to the applicable Advance and has PRI schedule and book studio time. Whether the Advance is the recording fund out of which those costs are met, or a payment separate from them, is only answerable by reading the two together.

The right to deduct "from any and all monies payable hereunder, except mechanical royalty payments" leaves "hereunder" and "monies payable" unbounded — it is not said whether they reach royalties cross-collateralized from the Polydor Agreements under paragraph 6.04 or amounts other than royalties. The single express carve-out for mechanical royalties invites an expressio unius reading that everything else is fair game.

The royalty base, "the lowest wholesale price ... payable by PRI's customers," is nowhere defined and is not the "Royalty Base" used throughout Article 7 of the Agreement, so it is unclear whose price, at what time, and net of what discounts sets the figure. "Lowest" invites a reading keyed to the most favoured customer as against the ordinary published wholesale price.

The clause reads "payable by PRI's customers is respect of such Audio-Visual Device," a mechanical error for "in respect of." The enumerated territory "Benelux" is also left undefined, so which countries fall under (b) rather than the residual rate in 7.11(c) is not fixed by the text.

The royalty percentage for territories outside the United States and those listed in 7.11(b) is struck through and hand-altered, so the operative rate cannot be read from the instrument. What rate the parties agreed for the residual territories is exactly what a court would have to determine.

A CD/Video is defined in added 13.04(g) as a Phonograph Record in laser-read compact disc form, so it also falls within paragraph 7.04(a) of the Agreement, which gives PRI an option as to how compact disc royalties are computed, and within the 7.02 Album escalations. Which of 7.12(a) and 7.04(a)/7.02 governs sales of a CD/Video in the United States is not resolved.

The numerator of the fraction is "the royalty rate set forth in this agreement for Net Sales of disc Albums sold by PRI for distribution in the applicable country," but paragraph 7.03 of the Agreement sets no country rates except for Japan — it fixes fractions (3/4, 2/3, 1/2) of the otherwise applicable United States rate. The denominator is likewise unstable because the United States Album rate escalates with unit sales under 7.02(b)-(e).

"The lowest wholesale price, exclusive of excise, sales and similar taxes, payable by PRI's customers" is undefined and departs from the "Royalty Base" mechanism used elsewhere in Article 7 of the Agreement. Whether "lowest" means the lowest price charged to any customer anywhere or the standard wholesale price for the configuration is left open.

The exclusion covers only "automatic" free goods as set forth in paragraph 13.15(a)(ii), leaving discretionary, special-sales-plan or discount free goods apparently still applicable to CD/Videos. The qualifier "automatic" thus creates a specific-versus-general problem about which free goods programs may reduce CD/Video royalties.

"Concert Video" is already a defined term in paragraph 5.02(b) of the Agreement, meaning any Audio-Visual Recording of Artist taped at one time running thirty minutes or more, and this paragraph re-defines it as the single Red Star recording. The two definitions cannot both be given effect, and 5.02(b)'s consent and good-faith-negotiation regime turns on which one is used.

Paragraph 5.02(a)(ii) of the Agreement obliges PRI to produce a Video "at its own expense" corresponding to one Master Recording on the applicable Album; deeming the purchase of a long-form concert film to satisfy that obligation cannot be squared with 8(c), which turns the purchase price into a recoupable Advance charged to the artist. The hedge "any obligation PRI may have" also leaves it open whether the 5.02(a)(ii) obligation was ever triggered for this Album.

PRI's absolute discretion to exploit or refrain from exploiting the Concert Video cannot easily be squared with 8(c), which charges the artist with the costs as Advances recoupable from his royalties, and with the royalty provisions 7.11 and 7.12 that are his only return on the video. Read against the displaced 5.02(b), which required mutual consent and good-faith negotiation, the scope of "sole discretion" is what is in issue.

Treating all amounts paid in connection with the Concert Video as Advances conflicts with paragraph 6.03 of the Agreement, which deems only one-half of video production costs Advances, and with the proviso in 5.02(a)(ii) barring recoupment of production costs of Audio-Visual Recordings in excess of two per Album. Which regime governs the Red Star purchase and its editing and post-production costs is unresolved.

The proviso states only that fifty percent of such costs "shall be recoupable from audio-only Record royalties," and says nothing about whether the other fifty percent is recoupable from audio-visual or other income or not recoupable at all. "Audio-only Record royalties" is itself undefined against the Agreement's royalty categories.

"All forms of reproductions of Audio-Visual Recordings, excluding CD/Video, now or hereafter known, manufactured or distributed primarily for home and/or juke box use and/or use on or in means of transportation" leaves "primarily" unmeasured and the placement of "now or hereafter known" unclear as to what it modifies. Whether later-developed formats and non-home configurations fall inside the definition, and so attract the 7.11 rates, turns on those words.

Defining a CD/Video as a Phonograph Record in compact disc form that "may ... include additional audio-only Sides" leaves it straddling amended 13.03(a), which excludes CD/Video from Audio-Visual Devices, and the Album/compact disc royalty provisions 7.02 and 7.04 of the Agreement. Which royalty applies to a disc that is mostly audio-only Sides is not resolved by reading 13.04(g) with 7.12.

The definition of "or equivalent" is circular and open-ended: it lists pre-recorded tape and compact disc and then sweeps in "any other Record equivalent," defining the phrase by itself. The catch-all sitting behind two enumerated configurations invites an ejusdem generis dispute over which formats it reaches.

The wholesale importation of the Agreement's definitions collides with this letter's own usages — it addresses "you" personally while the Agreement's operative party is "Grantor," and paragraph 8 gives "Concert Video" a meaning different from that in 5.02(b) of the Agreement. Which definition controls where the two instruments use the same word differently is left unstated.

"Except as expressly or by necessary implication modified hereby" supplies no standard for what counts as modification by necessary implication, so which of the Agreement's terms survive this amendment is left at large. The problem bites on provisions such as 5.02(a)(ii), 6.03 and 4.01(c)-(d), which the amendment touches only obliquely.
